blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — antiseizure-medication planning before pregnancy
stem: A client with epilepsy who takes an antiseizure medication is planning pregnancy. Which statement by the client shows correct understanding of preconception medication planning?

options.A: I will stop the antiseizure medication while trying to conceive and restart it after the first trimester to minimize fetal exposure.
options.B: I will arrange a preconception review to optimize my medication and dose, and discuss taking at least 0.4 mg of folic acid daily before conception and during pregnancy.
options.C: I will keep the current regimen without preconception review and wait until pregnancy is confirmed before discussing medication or folic acid changes.
options.D: I will avoid folic acid while taking an antiseizure medication because supplementation is not recommended with these medications during pregnancy.

rationale: The current AAN/AES/SMFM practice guideline recommends choosing antiseizure medications and doses that optimize both seizure control and fetal outcomes at the earliest possible opportunity before conception. It also recommends at least 0.4 mg of folic acid daily before conception and during pregnancy for people with epilepsy who are treated with an antiseizure medication. Therefore B is the best answer. A promotes an unsupervised treatment interruption that is not recommended and can jeopardize seizure control. C misses the guideline's preconception optimization window and delays folic-acid planning. D directly contradicts the folic-acid recommendation.
educational_objective: Teach clients with epilepsy who are planning pregnancy to obtain preconception review of antiseizure medication choice and dose and to discuss at least 0.4 mg of folic acid daily before conception and during pregnancy rather than changing therapy independently.
source_organization: American Academy of Neurology (AAN), American Epilepsy Society (AES), and Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine (SMFM)
source_document_title: Teratogenesis, Perinatal, and Neurodevelopmental Outcomes After In Utero Exposure to Antiseizure Medication: Practice Guideline From the AAN, AES, and SMFM
source_version_date: Published online May 15, 2024; Neurology June 2024; PubMed record last revised June 17, 2026
source_locator: Abstract > major recommendations: clinicians should recommend antiseizure medications and doses that optimize seizure control and fetal outcomes at the earliest possible opportunity preconceptionally; clinicians should prescribe at least 0.4 mg of folic acid supplementation daily preconceptionally and during pregnancy to people with epilepsy of childbearing potential treated with an antiseizure medication.
source_claim_supported: For people with epilepsy taking an antiseizure medication, medication choice and dose should be optimized before conception when possible, and at least 0.4 mg of folic acid daily is recommended before conception and during pregnancy.
blueprint_locator: Printed p. 38, Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: review pertinent medication data; educate clients about medications; evaluate medication appropriateness, contraindications, and risks; provide safe medication care integrated with reproductive-health needs.
candidate_reasons_resolved: Rewrote the item as four realistic client statements rather than one long comprehensive answer against obviously false short distractors.
Removed isolated absolute wording and balanced option structure and length while preserving one guideline-supported best response.
Kept the precise 0.4-mg folic-acid recommendation directly tied to the published guideline and avoided any unsourced medication-switch schedule.
audit_note: Independent adversarial review confirms B uniquely reflects both major preconception recommendations. A encourages unsupervised treatment interruption, C delays the recommended preconception review and folic-acid planning, and D contradicts the guideline's folic-acid recommendation. Although B remains modestly longer, the alternatives are all substantive full teaching statements and answer length is not a reliable cue; no second defensible answer remains.
